text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- One of six Swedes fit for work gets subsidies of some kind, but with the new proposal for social benefits, which will be presented by Health & Social Affairs Minister Margot Wallstrom on Thursday, the dependance on subsidies will decrease. But the number of poor will not decline.
- The North Sea could face an ecological collapse, mainly because of intensive fishing. The situation is most serious for cod, but also herring and mackerell are in danger.

- The minority Social Democratic government is likely to present an extensive job package in the spring budget on April 15 in a move to win voter support ahead of general elections in the autumn of 1998. The government has promised to halve unemployment until the year 2000, but unemployment has remained high with the February figure showing 8.8 percent without any job. Support for the Social Democrats has fallen with the latest poll showing 26.5 percent of voters favouring the party, down from 45 percent in the 1994 election.
- Certain viruses in pigs, which at laboratories can infect human cells, have been discovered by at least two research groups. This increases worries about transplanting pigs' organs to humans.

- The Danish newspaper Sondagsavisen intends to grow abroad and the first step will be to launch a newspaper, Weekend Avisen, in the Stockholm region on Saturday. The new paper, which will be free of charge and totally dependant on advertisments, will be 50-50 owned by the Danish newspaper and Swedish newspaper Dagens Nyheter. Eventually the owners aim for the new newspaper to cover most of Sweden.

- This summer the new chief executive of Swedish medical and technical gas group AGA AB, Lennart Selander, will decide if company headquarters will be moved abroad. In addition, the company will look into expanding in Asia, mainly by considering acquisitions of small and middle-sized companies.

- Volvo Construction Equipment (VCE), the construction machinery group of Swedish automotive group AB Volvo, will keep expanding, despite the German market being weak. The company has 20 percent of its turnover in Germany.

- Automotive group AB Volvo and state-owned telecoms group Telia AB are the first Swedish companies to invest employees' pension savings on the stock exchange. Telia has in a short period of time built a portfolio of Swedish shares worth 1.4 billion crowns. Volvo has just started to invest its employees' pension savings and has Swedish shares worth 300 million crowns. If all other Swedish companies would follow suit, a total of 83 billion crowns could be invested in funds, which then buy shares and bonds.

- Only one out of seven Swedish funds beat the Stockholm Stock Exchange's general index in 1996. There is still just one Swedish fund company, Erik Penser Fonder, that offers an index fund which follows a share index at a low administration cost.
